meta_desc: Teach grade 3 multiplication word problems the easy way: spot equal groups, arrays and times-as-many, write the sentence, and try a free 8-question quiz.
excerpt: The hard part of a multiplication word problem in Grade 3 is not the times table — it is knowing the story means multiply. Here is how to spot equal groups, arrays and times-as-many, and turn each one into a clean number sentence.
author: Sachin Sharma
content:
Give a Grade 3 child the sum 6 × 8 and most will answer 48 without much fuss. Now dress it up — ‘Riya packs 6 boxes and puts 8 pencils in each box’ — and half the class reaches for addition, or freezes. That gap is the whole challenge of grade 3 multiplication word problems: the times table is the easy bit; deciding that the story means multiply is where children stumble. Once a child can name the type of story, the number sentence almost writes itself.

There are really only three story types a Grade 3 child needs to recognise, and I teach them in this exact order. Get the first one solid and the other two fall into place.

The three stories that mean multiply

Every Grade 3 multiplication word problem I have set in eight years of tutoring is a version of one of these. Say the type out loud before touching the numbers — that naming step is what separates confident solvers from guessers.

Story typeWhat it sounds likeExampleSentence
Equal groups‘___ boxes of ___’, ‘___ each’6 boxes of 8 pencils6 × 8 = 48
Array / rows‘___ rows of ___’, a grid4 rows of 5 chairs4 × 5 = 20
Times as many‘___ times as many’3 times as many as 73 × 7 = 21

1. Equal groups — the anchor

This is the picture behind every other type, so spend the most time here. The clue words are the small ones parents skim past: each, every, per, and the phrase ‘boxes of’. When Riya packs 6 boxes with 8 pencils in each, the groups are equal, so we multiply the number of groups by the size of each group: 6 × 8 = 48 pencils.

I ask children to draw it — six loops, eight dots in each. Nobody who draws the loops adds by mistake. The drawing also settles the classic worry: does it matter whether you write 6 × 8 or 8 × 6? For the answer, no — both give 48. For the story, 6 × 8 reads as ‘six groups of eight’, which matches, so I nudge them to write it that way. It builds good habits for later grades.

2. Arrays and rows

An array is just equal groups lined up in a neat grid — chairs in a hall, tiles on a floor, sweets in a tray. ‘4 rows of 5 chairs’ is 4 groups of 5, so 4 × 5 = 20. The reason arrays deserve their own lesson is that they make the ‘order does not change the answer’ idea obvious: turn the grid a quarter turn and 4 rows of 5 becomes 5 rows of 4, still 20 chairs. Seeing that once is worth ten times being told it.

3. Times as many

This is the trickiest of the three because it hides inside a comparison. ‘Arjun has 7 marbles. Meera has 3 times as many’ is not addition — the words ‘times as many’ are a flashing signal to multiply: 3 × 7 = 21. Children who have only met ‘boxes of’ problems often add 3 and 7 here, so I flag this phrase specifically. If the words ‘times as many’ appear, multiply. No exceptions at this level.

From story to number sentence in three steps

Once the type is named, the rest is a routine. I have children chant it, because a routine under pressure beats cleverness every time.

  • Name the type — equal groups, array, or times as many.
  • Find the two numbers — how many groups, and how big is each group.
  • Write it as groups × size, then solve with a known table fact.

For ‘8 packets, 9 stickers in each’: type is equal groups; numbers are 8 and 9; sentence is 8 × 9 = 72. Three steps, no guessing.

Solving with the tables to 10 — and a little beyond

Most Grade 3 problems keep products under 100 and stay inside the tables to 10, which is exactly why mastering those tables pays off. But NCERT also nudges children toward simple two-digit × one-digit sums like 12 × 4, and the trick is to split the big number. For 12 × 4, think 10 × 4 = 40 and 2 × 4 = 8, then add: 40 + 8 = 48. A store selling 12 boxes with 4 laddoos in each has 48 laddoos. Splitting the tens and ones like this is the bridge to the column method they meet next year, so it is worth practising even when the answer feels reachable other ways.

A quick estimate keeps answers honest

Before solving, I ask ‘roughly how big?’ If 12 × 4 should be around 12 four times — clearly more than 40, less than 60 — then a child who writes 16 (having added) can catch their own slip. Estimation is not extra work; it is a free error-check.

The mistakes to head off early

Two errors show up again and again, and both are about reading, not arithmetic. First, adding when the story says multiply — usually because the child rushed past ‘each’ or ‘times as many’. Second, multiplying the wrong pair of numbers when a problem throws in a spare figure to distract (a price, a leftover). Underlining the two numbers that go with the groups, and crossing out the rest, fixes both. Honestly, most word-problem marks are lost to careless reading, not to weak tables.

Try the quiz, then the printable practice

Below is a free 8-question quiz built only from these three story types — equal groups, arrays, and times as many — with products that stay in the tables to 10 plus one gentle 2-digit stretch. Let your child name the type before choosing an answer, then read each explanation together. quiz.intro: Eight questions on the three story types that mean multiply: equal groups, arrays and times as many. Name the type, pick an answer, then press Check my score.
quiz.about: Grade 3 multiplication word problems, products to about 100

questions.q: Riya packs 6 boxes and puts 8 pencils in each box. How many pencils in all?
questions.explanation: Equal groups: 6 boxes of 8 means 6 × 8 = 48 pencils.

questions.q: A hall has 4 rows of chairs with 5 chairs in each row. How many chairs?
questions.explanation: An array of 4 rows of 5 is 4 × 5 = 20 chairs.

questions.q: Arjun has 7 marbles. Meera has 3 times as many. How many does Meera have?
questions.explanation: The words 'times as many' mean multiply: 3 × 7 = 21 marbles.

questions.q: A shop sells 12 boxes of laddoos with 4 laddoos in each box. How many laddoos?
Which word in a problem is a signal to multiply?
questions.explanation: 'Each' points to equal groups, so you multiply the number of groups by the size of each group.

questions.q: 8 packets have 9 stickers in each packet. How many stickers altogether?
questions.explanation: Equal groups: 8 packets of 9 means 8 × 9 = 72 stickers.

questions.q: A tray holds 5 rows of 6 sweets. How many sweets does the tray hold?
A rickshaw carries 3 people. How many people can 7 rickshaws carry?
questions.explanation: Equal groups: 7 rickshaws with 3 each means 7 × 3 = 21 people.

faq.q: How do I know a word problem means multiply, not add?
faq.a: Look for equal groups. Phrases like 'each', 'per', 'boxes of', 'rows of' and 'times as many' signal multiplication. If every group is the same size, you multiply the number of groups by the size of each group.

faq.q: Does the order of the numbers matter, like 6 × 8 versus 8 × 6?
faq.a: For the answer, no — both give 48. For matching the story, writing 'groups × size' (6 boxes of 8 as 6 × 8) builds a good habit that helps in later grades.

faq.q: How do you solve a 2-digit times 1-digit problem like 12 × 4?
faq.a: Split the bigger number into tens and ones: 10 × 4 = 40 and 2 × 4 = 8, then add to get 48. This is the bridge to the column method in Grade 4.

faq.q: Why does my child add when the problem clearly means multiply?
faq.a: Usually careless reading — they skip past 'each' or 'times as many'. Have them name the story type and underline the two numbers before writing anything. Drawing equal groups also stops the mistake.
